Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would require masters of domestic commercial vessels to count passengers twice on each trip.
The Australian Maritime Safety Authority would be directed to write a rule mandating a headcount when the voyage starts and another when it ends.
The requirement would not apply to Class 4 vessels, vessels used for public transport, or vessels longer than 24 metres.
The bill would increase the required passenger headcounts from one to two per voyage.
It would exclude certain vessel types from the new headcount requirement.
It would task the Australian Maritime Safety Authority with creating the instrument to enforce the rule.
Masters of domestic commercial vessels and their passengers are affected, as well as the Australian Maritime Safety Authority.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-02-10.93.1) to agree with the main idea of the bill. This means they can now discuss it in more detail. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). ### What is the bill's main idea? The [purpose of the bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/s1248) is "to require masters of certain vessels to conduct two headcounts of passengers, one at the start of a voyage and one at the end." ### Background to the bill According to the bill's [explanatory memorandum](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fems%2Fs1248_ems_55211ee9-0b50-4a0a-9cd9-6a5247efaf5d%22;rec=0): > *This bill is needed to avoid a similar case occurring to that which happened with the [tragic loss of Mr Damien Mills](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2017-06-06/inquest-into-death-of-damien-mills-on-perth-cruise/8593166) when he fell off the back of a boat undetected and died in 2014. Had the master of that vessel conducted a headcount when the boat got back to Fremantle, they would have realised that Mr Mills was missing and they could have alerted the appropriate authorities. WA Water Police, in giving evidence to the Senate’s Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee’s inquiry into the performance of the Australian Maritime Safety Authority, stated that had they been made aware that Mr Mills had fallen overboard at the time the vessel docked, they would have had a very strong chance of finding him alive.*

Migration Amendment (Regulation of Migration Agents) Bill 2019 and another - in Committee - Independent review

The Migration Amendment (Regulation of Migration Agents) Bill 2019 deregulates the migration advice industry by removing lawyers with unrestricted practising certificates from Migration Agents Registration Authority regulation, extending registration periods via delegated legislation, repealing redundant provisions, closing a loophole on incomplete applications, requiring notification of changes in non-commercial registration status, and expanding definitions to include assistance with character-based visa revocation.

The bill amends the Migration Agents Registration Application Charge Act 1997 to require migration agents who originally registered as non-commercial but later provide commercial immigration assistance to pay a pro-rata adjusted charge, complementing changes ensuring the non-commercial charge is only available to genuine non-profit providers.

Labor did not oppose the Migration Amendment (Regulation of Migration Agents) Bill 2019 and related charge bill, but moved a second reading amendment criticising the government for taking over five years to act on the 2014 Kendall review recommendations. The bills remove the requirement for lawyers with unrestricted practising certificates to register as migration agents, instead regulating them through state and territory professional bodies.

The speaker argued that the Migration Amendment (Regulation of Migration Agents) Bill 2019 and the Migration Agents Registration Application Charge Amendment (Rates of Charge) Bill 2019 would cut red tape by removing dual regulation for legal practitioners, saving small practices from unnecessary costs and training. The bills remove unrestricted lawyers from Migration Agents Registration Authority regulation, give restricted lawyers two years to transition, and adjust registration charges for non-commercial migration advice providers.

The speaker supported the Migration Amendment (Regulation of Migration Agents) Bill and the Migration Agents Registration Application Charge Amendment (Rates of Charge) Bill 2019, which remove dual registration requirements for lawyers providing immigration assistance and update definitions, but argued the bills are long overdue—based on 2014 recommendations and first introduced in 2017—and backed Labor’s amendments for Senate scrutiny.

The speaker argued the bills partially implement recommendation 1 of the 2014 OMARA review, removing lawyers from the migration agents regulatory scheme to allow legal practitioners to register as migration agents, and noted previous support for the legislation.

The Migration Amendment (Regulation of Migration Agents) Bill 2019 removes legal practitioners with unrestricted practising certificates from the OMARA regulatory scheme and allows OMARA to refuse incomplete applications, while the Migration Agents Registration Application Charge Amendment (Rates of Charges) Bill 2019 adjusts charges for agents providing commercial immigration assistance.

If so, the bill will become law. ### What is the main idea of the bill? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1920a/20bd104): > *The purpose of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Superannuation, Your Choice) Bill 2019 (the Bill) is to amend the Superannuation Guarantee (Administration) Act 1992 (SGAA) to ensure employees under new workplace determinations or enterprise agreements have an opportunity to choose the superannuation fund for their compulsory employer contributions.*

The speaker argued for the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Superannuation, Your Choice) Bill 2019, which from 1 July 2020 gives workers under enterprise agreements or awards the right to choose their own superannuation fund, and criticised the opposition for proposing $387 billion in new taxes at the last election.

Labor referred the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Superannuation, Your Choice) Bill 2019 to a Senate inquiry over concerns that vulnerable employees could be forced into underperforming funds, while also criticising the government's record on superannuation and supporting consumer protections such as APRA heat maps.

The speaker argued that industry super funds squander and take control of Australians' retirement savings, criticising the member for Kingsford Smith for defending them during debate on the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Superannuation, Your Choice) Bill 2019.

The speaker argued in favour of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Superannuation, Your Choice) Bill 2019, which gives workers under new workplace determinations or enterprise agreements the right to choose their superannuation fund from July 1, 2020. They highlighted that Australia’s superannuation system holds $2.8 trillion in assets, noted that 2.85 million Australians were underpaid $5.9 billion in superannuation, and pointed out that women retire with significantly lower balances than men, with 34% of single women over 60 living in poverty.

Labor supported the bill to allow employees under new enterprise agreements to choose their superannuation fund, arguing for stronger consumer protections and warning the change could undermine collective choice in industry funds, which have historically outperformed retail funds. The member for Corangamite also criticised the government for failing to address employer non-payment of superannuation and for freezing the Super Guarantee.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Superannuation, Your Choice) Bill 2019 would allow banks to access workers' retirement savings by removing the ability to collectively bargain over superannuation funds, and compared it to the WorkChoices era. They noted that industry funds, often negotiated through enterprise agreements, deliver better returns than bank-run funds, and accused the government of acting on donations from big banks.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Superannuation, Your Choice) Bill 2019, which gives workers the choice of superannuation fund for workplace determinations and enterprise agreements from 1 July 2020 and closes a loophole allowing employers to claim salary sacrifice super as employer contributions. The speaker cited complaints from casual university staff forced into UniSuper, where fees eroded their balances.

Labor supported the bill’s intent to give employees choice of superannuation fund but reserved its position pending a Senate inquiry, citing concerns about unintended consequences and the government’s ideological opposition to industry super funds. The speaker noted that only 7.4% of employees under enterprise agreements currently lack choice, and supported amendments highlighting inadequate retirement savings and the legislated super guarantee rise to 12% by 2025.

The speaker opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Superannuation, Your Choice) Bill 2019, arguing it would harm working Australians by offering a false choice that could lead to lower retirement incomes, and characterised conservative policy as a "double whammy" of flat wages and no increase in superannuation contributions. They supported referring the bill to a Senate committee for further scrutiny.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Superannuation, Your Choice) Act 2020

The usual second reading motion is "that the bill be read for a second time", which is parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill. The amendment was introduced by Shortland MP [Pat Conroy](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/shortland/pat_conroy) (Labor). ### Amendment text > *That all words after 'That' be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *'whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House:* > > *(1) notes that Australia's Official Development Assistance (ODA) investments are an important way of advancing Australia's interests, projecting our values and tackling global poverty;* > > *(2) expresses concern that since 2014 Coalition Governments have cut $11.8 billion from the foreign aid budget with the result that Australia's ODA investments are now at a record low as a share of Gross National Income;* > > *(3) agrees that active and engaged participation in multilateral institutions, including multilateral development institutions, is essential for advancing Australia's interests in a stable, secure and prosperous international environment; and* > > *(4) expresses concern that the Prime Minister's recent public attacks on global institutions are contrary to Australia's interests in an international rules-based order supported by multilateral institutions which promote economic growth, global security and human development'*

The majority voted against a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-06-10.8.1) introduced by South Australian Senator [Penny Wong](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/penny_wong) (Labor), which means it failed. This motion would have amended the usual [second reading motion](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/): that the bill be read for a second time. Reading something for a second time is the same as agreeing with the main idea of the bill. ### Motion text > *At the end of the motion, add:* > > *", but the Senate:* > > *(a) notes that Australia's Official Development Assistance (ODA) investments are an important way of advancing Australia’s interests, projecting our values and tackling global poverty;* > > *(b) expresses its concern that:* > >> *(i) since 2014, Coalition governments have cut $11.8 billion from the foreign aid budget, with the result that Australia's ODA investments are now at a record low as a share of Gross National Income, and* >> >> *(ii) the Prime Minister's promotion of negative globalism is contrary to Australia's interests in an international rules-based order supported by multilateral institutions, which promote economic growth, global security and human development; and* > > *(c) agrees that active and engaged participation in multilateral institutions, including multilateral development institutions, is essential for advancing Australia’s interests in a stable, secure and prosperous international environment".*

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2020-06-10.13.1) to pass the bill. In other words, they voted to read it for a [third time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). Because it had already been read for a third time in the House of Representatives, it will now become law. ### What does the bill do? The bill was [introduced to do the following](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6437): > *Appropriates money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund to meet certain Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations in relation to the World Bank’s International Development Association and debt relief schemes, including the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries Initiative and the Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative; the Asian Development Bank’s Asian Development Fund; the Global Environment Facility Trust Fund; and the Multilateral Fund for the Implementation of the Montreal Protocol.*

The bill appropriates money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund to meet Australia's existing and future obligations to six multilateral funds: the World Bank's International Development Association, its debt relief schemes (Heavily Indebted Poor Countries Initiative and Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative), the Asian Development Bank's Asian Development Fund, the Global Environment Facility Trust Fund, and the Multilateral Fund for the Implementation of the Montreal Protocol, providing a standing appropriation for three- to four-year replenishment cycles with payments over three to ten years.

Labor supported the bill but moved an amendment expressing concern that Coalition governments have cut $11.8 billion from foreign aid since 2014, bringing Australia's aid to a record low of 0.18% of GNI, and that the Prime Minister's public attacks on multilateral institutions undermine Australia's interests in a rules-based international order.

The speaker, a Labor MP, announced support for the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019, which funds multilateral development funds including the International Development Association and Asian Development Fund, but criticised the government for cutting $11.8 billion from aid since 2013, reducing Australia's ODA to 0.19% of GNI—the lowest since 1961—and accused Prime Minister Morrison of hypocrisy for attacking multilateral institutions while supporting this bill.

The speaker supported the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019 but criticised the government for cutting $11.8 billion from Australia's aid budget since 2013, resulting in the lowest share of national income for aid under any Liberal prime minister.

The speaker argued that while the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019 has bipartisan support, the Coalition government has cut $12 billion from aid since 2013, reducing it to the lowest level on record, including halving aid to Pakistan to $19 million and cutting Cambodia's aid to $43 million. The speaker urged a larger aid program and global leadership, citing Labor's past achievements like the Mining for Development program and framing the Coalition's approach as a "little-Australia" strategy under the "straiteners."

The speaker supported the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019 and an amendment moved by the member for Shortland, while criticising the Prime Minister’s remarks about “unaccountable internationalist bureaucracy” and “negative globalism” as vague and lacking specifics. They noted that global extreme poverty fell to 10% in 2015, with over a billion people raised out of poverty.

The speaker argued that Australia must meet its multilateral development fund commitments and criticised the Coalition government for cutting $11.8 billion from foreign aid since 2013, with the aid budget projected to fall to 0.19% of gross national income by 2022-23. Specific cuts include a 50% reduction in aid to Indonesia and 41% in education spending, while contrasting the UK's 0.7% GNI target.

The speaker argued that Australia's aid budget has been cut by 27% from 2013 levels, including a $700 million cut in 2014 and the closure of AusAID, while spending on pets ($12.2 billion annually) far exceeds aid ($3.8–3.9 billion). He called for a bipartisan agreement to increase aid spending toward 0.5% of gross national income, citing specific cuts to programs in Pakistan and Africa/Middle East, and criticised the government for neglecting climate change commitments and using positive isolationism as a policy.

The speaker supported the amendment to guarantee Australia's contributions to six multilateral aid funds but criticised the government for cutting $11.8 billion from development assistance since 2013, reducing aid to 0.19% of GNI—the lowest in history—and citing a 41% cut to education programs, a 32% cut to health programs, and the termination of aid to Pakistan after 70 years.

The speaker argued in support of the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations (Special Appropriation) Bill 2019, stating that Australian aid saves lives and is in Australia's national interest. They criticised the government for cutting $11.8 billion from the aid budget since 2013, reducing aid to 0.19% of gross national income—the lowest in history—and named specific funds covered by the bill, including the International Development Association, Asian Development Fund, and Global Environment Facility Trust Fund.

The speaker supported the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019, which authorises around $350 million annually for multilateral initiatives, and criticised the government for $11.8 billion in cumulative aid cuts, including a 10% cut to East Timor, a 50% cut to Indonesia, and an 86% cut to health funding in Indonesia.

Labor supported the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019 but criticised the coalition government for cutting $11.8 billion from aid since 2013, including specific reductions to Indonesia, Vietnam, Vanuatu, and other nations, while arguing the cuts undermine Australia's international standing and security.

The speaker supported the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019 but criticised the government for cutting foreign aid by $1.5 billion annually since 2013, including 41% from education and 32% from health, and specific reductions to Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines, Laos, Cambodia, and several Pacific islands, arguing these cuts undermine Australia's national interest and regional influence.

Australian aid spending has fallen to 0.22% of gross national income, with $11.8 billion cut since 2013, and the speaker argued for increased aid to Pacific neighbours and urged that funding under the bill be conditional on not using chrysotile asbestos in construction projects.

The member supported the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019 but criticised six consecutive aid budget cuts, noting funding is frozen at $4 billion (0.21% of GNI), and urged the government to adopt the bipartisan committee’s recommendation to increase aid to 0.5% of GNI within five years and 0.7% within ten.

Labor supported the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019, but argued the government's $11.8 billion in foreign aid cuts had reduced Australia's aid to 0.19% of gross national income—a record low—and specifically criticised cuts to health and education in Pacific nations including Samoa, Vanuatu and Timor-Leste.

Labor supported the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019 and the amendments moved by the member for Shortland. The speaker argued that since 2014, coalition governments have cut $11.8 billion from the foreign aid budget, reducing Australia's ODA to a record low of 0.19% of gross national income, and criticised cuts to health funding in Pacific nations including a 75% cut to the Cook Islands, 22% to Fiji, 13% to the Solomon Islands, and 36% to Samoa.

The speaker argued that the Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations Bill 2019 is a standing appropriation to meet Australia's commitments to multilateral development organisations, noting the Morrison government's $4 billion aid budget includes a record $1.4 billion for the Pacific and $450 million in humanitarian funding.
Official Development Assistance Multilateral Replenishment Obligations (Special Appropriation) Act 2020

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2020-02-24.40.1) to pass the [bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6413) in the Senate. Because it had already passed in the House, it will now become law. ### What does this bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1920a/20bd075), the bill: > *proposes amendments to superannuation and related tax laws to encourage the recovery of unpaid Superannuation Guarantee (SG) by introducing a temporary amnesty from late payment penalties for employers who disclose that they have underpaid SG in the past.*

The speaker moved an amendment to reject the Treasury Laws Amendment (Recovering Unpaid Superannuation) Bill 2019, arguing it provides an amnesty for employers who have not paid superannuation for 26 years and that the government is not doing enough to combat theft of workers' entitlements. The amendment calls on the government to help unions protect workers from superannuation theft and to end policy uncertainty by committing to legislated increases to the superannuation guarantee.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Recovering Unpaid Superannuation) Bill 2019 provides a business amnesty for unpaid superannuation, improves system integrity through expanded Single Touch Payroll, and is backed by $133.7 million for ATO compliance. He contrasted this approach with the opposition's focus on grandstanding rather than practical solutions.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Recovering Unpaid Superannuation) Bill 2019 as a small step, but noted only $230 million of the estimated $6 billion in unpaid super would be recovered, warned of moral hazard, and called for a 10-year moratorium on future amnesties, better ATO funding, and listing superannuation under the National Employment Standards.

The speaker argued that the ATO’s Single Touch Payroll will identify unpaid superannuation more quickly, and dismissed industry super’s multibillion-dollar figure as unverified. They also noted that the member for Whitlam declined to provide the source of his research and numbers.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Recovering Unpaid Superannuation) Act 2020
